function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the task.  
I’ve also included the exact file contents that should be added to the repository.

> **⚠️ Important** – I can’t actually clone, commit or push for you, but the commands below will do it on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

The repo contains a very small Node.js app (`index.js` + `package.json`).  
A minimal Dockerfile that works on any CI/CD runner looks like this:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# 1️⃣  Use a lightweight Node.js base image
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

# 2️⃣  Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# 3️⃣  Copy package files and install deps
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# 4️⃣  Copy the rest of the source
COPY . .

# 5️⃣  Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# 6️⃣  Default command
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small and fast.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees reproducible installs.  
> * The app listens on port **3000** (the default for many Node examples).  
> * No unnecessary build steps – perfect for CI.

> **Add it to the repo**

```bash
echo '...Dockerfile content...' > Dockerfile
```

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a single file `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can create the `k8s` folder if it doesn’t exist).

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **What to replace**  
> * `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` – e.g. `ghcr.io/zelarhq` or `docker.io/zelarhq`.  
> * If you want a `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer`, change `type:` accordingly.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions – Build & Push Docker Image

Create the workflow file at `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry (or Docker Hub)
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build \
            --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest \
            .

      # Push the image
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Why this workflow?**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to authenticate to GHCR (no extra secrets needed).  
> * Builds the image from the Dockerfile we just added.  
> * Pushes the image to `ghcr.io/<owner>/nodejs-welcome:latest`.

> **If you prefer Docker Hub** replace the login step with:

```yaml
- name: Log in to Docker Hub
  uses: docker/login-action@v3
  with:
    username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
    password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}
```

and adjust the image tags accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests & CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

### Quick sanity check

After pushing, you should see:

* A new **Actions** tab with a successful “Build & Push Docker Image” run.  
* The Docker image available in GHCR (or Docker Hub).  
* The `k8s/deployment.yaml` file in the repo.

You can now deploy the app to any Kubernetes cluster:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

That’s it! 🎉

Feel free to tweak the Docker image tag, registry, or Kubernetes settings to match your environment. If you hit any snags, let me know and I’ll help troubleshoot.
